engine: markdown
title: "rush plot"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
rush run -o mpg.csv 'ggplot2::mpg'
```

The `plot` command builds a [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) graphic
from your data. Choose columns with `--x`, `--y`, `--color`, and friends, and a
sensible geom is guessed for you (override it with `--geom`).

## Usage

```bash
rush plot [options] [--] [<file>...]
```

## Geom selection

When both `--x` and `--y` are given, `rush` guesses `geom_point`:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

When only `--x` is given, `rush` uses a histogram for a numeric column:

```{term}
rush plot -x mpg -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

and a bar chart for anything else (text, factors, logicals). For example, the
number of cars per class in ggplot2's `mpg` data:

```{term}
rush plot -x class -O ansi --width 72 mpg.csv
```

To count the distinct values of a numeric column, turn it into a factor:

```{term}
rush plot -x 'factor(cyl)' -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

The choice is made when the script runs, so the generated script contains `rush::geom_auto()`.

### `--geom` (`-g`)

Override the guessed geom. Any ggplot2 geom suffix works:

```{term}
rush plot -x mpg -g density -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

```{term}
rush plot -x cyl -y mpg -g boxplot -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -g smooth -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--geom-args`

Pass arguments to the geom, as R code. For example, `adjust` smooths a density
curve, and `alpha` makes it transparent:

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -f drv -g density --geom-args 'adjust = 2, alpha = 0.5' -n mpg.csv | grep -A 1 'ggplot('
```

```{term}
rush plot -x hwy -f drv -g density --geom-args 'adjust = 2, alpha = 0.5' mpg.csv > density.png
```

![](density.png){fig-alt="Smoothed, half-transparent density curves of highway mileage for each drive type in the mpg data set" width="500"}

Arguments set fixed values for the whole layer, unlike aesthetics such as
`--alpha`, which map a column. They also work with the guessed geom, e.g.
`--geom-args 'bins = 20'` for a histogram.

## Aesthetics

### `--color` (`-c`)

Map a column to the color aesthetic:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -c cyl -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--fill` (`-f`)

Map a column to fill (useful for histograms, bar charts, density plots):

```{term}
rush plot -x mpg -g density -f cyl --alpha 0.5 -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

In a bar chart, `--fill` stacks the counts of each group:

```{term}
rush plot -x class -f drv -O ansi --width 78 mpg.csv
```

### `--alpha` (`-a`)

Map a column to transparency. A constant such as `0.6` is mapped too, so it
adds a legend; to make a geom semi-transparent, use `--geom-args 'alpha = 0.6'`
instead:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --alpha 0.6 -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--size`

Map a column to point size, great for bubble charts:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --size hp -c cyl -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--shape`

Map a discrete column to point shape (a numeric column like `gear` needs
`factor()`, because ggplot2 can't map a continuous variable to shape):

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --shape 'factor(gear)' -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--group`

Group observations for geoms like `geom_line` that connect points:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --group cyl -g line -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--aes`

Pass additional aesthetics as `key=value` pairs:

```{term}
rush plot -x disp -y mpg --aes "label=cyl" -g text -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

## Axis and labels

### `--log`

Log-transform axes. Accepts `x`, `y`, or `xy`:

```{term}
rush plot -x hp -y mpg --log x -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--title`, `--xlab`, `--ylab`

Add axis labels and a title:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --title "Weight vs Fuel Economy" --xlab "Weight (1000 lbs)" --ylab "Miles per gallon" -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

## Facets

### One-sided formula (facet_wrap)

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --facets '~ cyl' -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### Two-sided formula (facet_grid) + `--margins`

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --facets 'am ~ cyl' --margins -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

## Pre- and post-processing

### `--pre`

Run code before the plot is built. Useful for data transformations:

```{term}
rush plot -x cyl -y avg_mpg --pre 'df <- df |> dplyr::summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg), .by = cyl)' -g col -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

### `--post`

Run code after the plot is built. The plot object is available as `p`:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg --post 'p + ggplot2::theme_minimal() + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm")' -O ansi --width 72 mtcars.csv
```

## Terminal output

When no `--output` is given and stdout is connected to a terminal, `rush`
renders the plot using
[devoutansi](https://github.com/jeroenjanssens/devoutansi). Use `-O ascii`
for plain-text output or `-O ansi` for colored output with ANSI escape codes:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ascii --width 70 mtcars.csv
```

### `--width`

Control how many characters wide the terminal art is (defaults to your
terminal width):

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ascii --width 40 mtcars.csv
```

### `--output-format ansi` / `ascii` (`-O`)

Without `-O`, the behaviour depends on whether stdout is a terminal. When it
is, `rush` renders ANSI art automatically. When it is not (piped or
redirected), it outputs raw PNG bytes by default. Use `-O ansi` to force
terminal art regardless:

```bash
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ansi mtcars.csv | less -R
```

The `ascii` variant uses plain ASCII characters without ANSI color codes,
which is useful for environments that do not support colors.

### Without a terminal

When stdout is not a terminal (for example, piped into another command), rush
outputs raw PNG bytes by default. You can redirect this to a file:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg mtcars.csv > scatter.png
```

This is the resulting `scatter.png`:

![](scatter.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of mpg against wt for the mtcars data set" width="500"}

## Saving plots

### `--output` (`-o`)

When `--output` points to a file, the plot is saved (device inferred from extension):

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -c cyl -o colored.png mtcars.csv
ls -la colored.png
```

### `--width`, `--height`, `--units`, `--dpi`

Control the saved image dimensions and resolution:

```{term}
rush plot -x wt -y mpg -o hires.png --width 10 --height 6 --units in --dpi 150 mtcars.csv
ls -la hires.png
```

## Reading from stdin

Without a file argument, `plot` reads from standard input:

```{term}
rush run 'head(df, 15)' mtcars.csv | rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ansi --width 72 -
```

## Multiple files

With multiple files, each is read into `dfs`. Use `--pre` to combine them
into `df` before plotting:

```{term}
echo "src,x,y
A,1,2
A,2,4
A,3,5" > a.csv
echo "src,x,y
B,1,3
B,2,2
B,3,6" > b.csv
rush plot -x x -y y -c src --pre 'df <- dplyr::bind_rows(dfs)' -O ansi --width 72 a.csv b.csv
rm -f a.csv b.csv
```

rush plot -h
